bridges.name: Multivariable calculus and local extrema
bridges.content_boundary: Recognize local minima, gradients, and Hessians in several variables; exclude proofs not represented in the Contract.

learning_outcomes.text: Recognize the neighbourhood-comparison meaning of a local minimum for a multivariable scalar function.
Assemble a gradient vector from first partial derivatives.
Recognize a Hessian as the matrix of second partial derivatives without applying an optimality test.

teaching_content.text: A point a is a local minimum of f when there is a neighbourhood of a in which f(a) <= f(x) for every nearby x.
For f(x_1, ..., x_d), compute each first partial derivative and assemble them as the gradient vector (partial f/partial x_1, ..., partial f/partial x_d)^T.
The Hessian H_f(x) is the square matrix whose (i,j) entry is the second partial derivative partial^2 f/(partial x_i partial x_j). Here it is used only to recognize the object and its dimensions.
For f(x,y) = x^2 + xy, the gradient is (2x+y, x)^T and the Hessian is [[2,1],[1,0]]. This example computes the objects but makes no minimum or definiteness claim.

excluded_content: Proof that differentiable local minima are stationary
Hessian definiteness tests or second-order optimality conditions
Gradient-descent updates, step sizes, or convergence claims

sources.title: Calculus of Several Variables, Lecture 20
sources.evidence_locator: Definitions 20.1 and 20.6 and the second-derivative/Taylor discussion on pp. 1-3 define the Hessian entries and local minima. BC-04 is a direct differentiation exercise using those definitions.

sources.title: 18.02 Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2007, Transcript - Lecture 12
sources.evidence_locator: Transcript p. 1 defines the gradient as the vector formed from all first partial derivatives; BC-04 directly applies that definition.

bridges.name: Euclidean norms and Lipschitz continuity
bridges.content_boundary: Interpret Euclidean norms and a Lipschitz bound for a vector-valued gradient; exclude function-value Lipschitzness.

learning_outcomes.text: Compute the Euclidean norm of a vector and use it to measure the distance between two vectors.
Read a vector-valued Lipschitz inequality as a bound on output change relative to input change.
Apply that interpretation when the vector-valued map is a gradient, without confusing it with function-value Lipschitzness.

teaching_content.text: For z in R^d, the Euclidean norm is ||z||_2 = sqrt(z^T z), and ||x-y||_2 measures Euclidean distance between x and y.
A vector-valued map G is L-Lipschitz when ||G(x)-G(y)||_2 <= L||x-y||_2. The inequality says that output vectors cannot separate faster than the input separation multiplied by L.
When G is the gradient map, compare the norm of the gradient difference with the norm of the point difference. This is a statement about changes in gradient vectors, not a bound on |f(x)-f(y)|.
For G(x)=2x, ||G(x)-G(y)||_2 = 2||x-y||_2, so the Lipschitz inequality holds with L=2. The example concerns a vector map only and introduces no gradient-descent claim.

excluded_content: The Descent Lemma or its proof

sources.title: Convex Optimization
sources.evidence_locator: Appendix A.1.1, p. 633 defines the standard inner product and Euclidean norm. BC-04 uses the norm's homogeneity in a direct scalar-multiplication calculation.

sources.title: CS 4787 Lecture 5: Smoothness and Strong Convexity
sources.evidence_locator: Section 'Lipschitz gradients and smoothness' states ||grad f(x)-grad f(y)|| <= L||x-y|| and interprets it as preventing the gradient from changing arbitrarily quickly. BC-04 is the same Lipschitz calculation for a generic vector map.

bridges.name: Inner products and convex sets
bridges.content_boundary: Interpret convex combinations and first-order inner-product inequalities; exclude advanced convex analysis.

learning_outcomes.text: Compute an inner product and recognize that its result is a scalar.
Form a convex combination and use it to recognize the defining closure property of a convex set.
Parse an expression of the form g^T(y-x) as an inner product with a displacement vector, without asserting an optimisation theorem.

teaching_content.text: For real vectors u and v of the same dimension, u^T v is the scalar sum of their componentwise products.
For x and y and a scalar theta in [0,1], theta x + (1-theta)y is a convex combination. A set is convex when it contains this combination for every pair of its points and every such theta.

To read g^T(y-x), first form the displacement d=y-x and then compute the scalar inner product g^T d. The sign describes alignment of g and the displacement; no convexity conclusion follows from this computation alone.
For x=(0,0)^T, y=(2,4)^T, and theta=1/4, theta x+(1-theta)y=(3/2,3)^T. If g=(1,-1)^T, then g^T(y-x)=-2. These are arithmetic interpretations, not a first-order convexity theorem.

excluded_content: The first-order characterization theorem for differentiable convex functions
Proofs of convexity or global optimality
Subgradients, separation theorems, and other advanced convex analysis

sources.title: Convex Optimization
sources.evidence_locator: Section 2.1, pp. 21-23 defines line segments, convex combinations, and convex sets; Appendix A.1.1, p. 633 defines the inner product. BC-03 and BC-04 directly apply these definitions.

bridges.name: Ratios and condition numbers
bridges.content_boundary: Compute and interpret L/mu and the lower bound kappa>=1; exclude other condition measures.

learning_outcomes.text: Compute kappa=L/mu for positive constants with L>=mu.
Interpret kappa as the multiplicative separation between L and mu without importing another condition-number definition.

teaching_content.text: For constants L>=mu>0, define the condition ratio kappa=L/mu. It is dimensionless when L and mu have the same units.
Because mu is positive, dividing L>=mu by mu gives kappa=L/mu>=1. A value near 1 means the two constants are close; a larger value means they are more widely separated multiplicatively.
If L=12 and mu=3, then kappa=4, so L is four times mu. If L=mu, then kappa=1.
The ratio requires mu>0. Do not treat L/mu as a finite condition ratio when mu=0.

excluded_content: Matrix, spectral, or numerical linear-algebra condition numbers
Step-size selection, acceleration, or stochastic optimisation claims

sources.title: CS 4787 Lecture 6: Gradient Descent
sources.evidence_locator: Lecture pp. 3-4 assumes positive strong-convexity and smoothness constants and defines the condition number kappa=L/mu. BC-02 through BC-04 are direct consequences and arithmetic examples under L>=mu>0, without using the lecture's convergence theorem.
